newsitem.title: USA: U.S. banks earned record $14.5 billion in Q1 1997.
newsitem.headline: U.S. banks earned record $14.5 billion in Q1 1997.

text.p: U.S. banks posted record net income of $14.5 billion in the first quarter, up 20 percent from $12.0 billion in the same quarter of 1996, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp reported on Tuesday.

Banks benefited from $24.7 billion in non-interest income, which includes everything from fees on checking accounts to commissions on mutual fund sales, up from $22.2 billion a year ago, the agency said.
Loan losses also grew in the first quarter, led by trouble in the credit card sector. Total losses for the quarter were $4.0 billion, up from $3.6 billion a year earlier.
A $560 million increase in credit card losses, to $2.8 billion for the quarter, more than accounted for the increase in total losses.
But banks continued to generate profits on credit cards despite the higher losses, FDIC chairman Andrew Hove said at a press briefing here.

"Loans to individuals in general, and credit card loans in particular, continue to be a highly profitable line of business for banks," Hove said. "The higher spreads on these loans more than offset the higher charge-offs rates they incur."
Hove said banks continued to expand their credit card loans base but the rate of growth had slowed.

Banks held $215.9 billion in credit card loans at the end of the quarter, up from $202.8 a year earlier. Loans securitized and sold rose to $164.9 billion from $135.4 billion, and unused committments of credit on credit cards rose to $1.47 trillion from $1.20 trillion.
Banks also increased their off-balance-sheet holdings of derivatives, financial instruments whose value is tied to the value of something else, such as a stock, commodity or interest rate index.
